item.title: [十字路口Crossing] OpenAI 和 Anthropic 共同看好的 FDE：AI 时代的新岗位出现，旧分工松动｜对谈 Rolling AI [中文]
item.description:
WHY YOU: The services-as-software question from the vendor's side of the table: two ex-BCG consultants who run an FDE-style AI services firm open with their revenue, profit and headcount (01:08), explain why AI sells as labor rather than software and why FDEs look like HR business partners placing 'digital employees' (02:19), lay out the three ways implementations die — CEO expectations, IT-led instead of business-led, incentives that don't change (32:01) — and close on whether the model is 'Service as Software' or 'Result as a Service', one-client-per-industry exclusivity, and why FDE firms may suit being owned rather than VC-funded (49:08). Listener comments dispute the firm's client count and scale, so treat the numbers as claims.
主播 Koji 对谈 Rolling AI 合伙人阿甘和刘开，聊 OpenAI 与 Anthropic 同日宣布的 FDE（前线部署工程师）岗位与企业 AI 落地的生意。01:08 快问快答：背景、公司、收入、利润、团队规模、过往经历；02:19 AI 是劳动力而非软件，FDE 像 HRBP 把'数字员工'放进企业，为何离开 BCG，MBB 在中国民企遇到的问题；08:22 第一个案例：乳企用 AI agent 服务约 600 万用户，营养师与目标用户之间约 200 倍的供给缺口，最难的是找到好的人类专家来训练 AI；19:58 FDE 要完成业务融合、知识治理、系统打通才能离场，好的 FDE 兼具问题诊断、人机协作和快速原型能力；25:09 SOP 意味着慢，总部从控制转向赋能，管理层级会被压缩；28:21 企业失败不是因为没用新技术——技术只占 AI 落地的不到三分之一；32:01 三种失败模式：CEO 期望不切实际、IT 主导而非业务主导、激励机制没有随技术改变；43:29 应届生能提供什么，如何判断商业 sense；46:49 实验室为何入场 FDE：数据与行业知识缺口是模型落地的主要障碍，ToB 本质是服务生意，JV 为何采用 PE 式结构；49:08 商业模式：FDE 公司更适合被 VC 持有而非被 VC 投资，一个行业只服务一家，未来是 Service as Software 还是 Result as a Service。约 55 分钟。

item.title: [42章经] 一个 AI 创始人的虚荣心、装，和愚昧之巅｜对谈 invoko.ai 创始人梦琪 [中文] [wildcard]
item.description:
WHY YOU: Candor in the Liblib mould: a founder who raised money, hit the 'peak of ignorance' and then the valley of despair as coding models got strong, walks through three pivot decisions that sounded coherent and were wrong — vertical agents (08:45), over-serving professional users (11:40), the wrong scenario (12:28) — asks whether many vertical-agent products are really staged for investors (17:30), contrasts two AI software business models, high-spend operations vs the gym model (18:45), and argues ToB isn't worth founding a company for (22:48). No revenue numbers and consumer-leaning, hence the wildcard tag, but it is the counter-case to every vertical-agent pitch you hear.
42章经主播曲凯对谈 invoko.ai 创始人梦琪（前字节跳动）。02:54 去年融到大钱的创业者该不该敬 Manus 一杯；03:45 三四月份一度觉得做软件是疯了；05:17 AI Coding 已经这么强，为什么跑出来的产品这么少；08:26 复盘转型路上的错误决策：08:45 ① 做垂直 Agent，11:40 ② 过度服务专业用户，12:28 ③ 选错场景；17:08 垂直 Agent 的两个结构性困境，17:30 很多 AI 产品是不是只是做给投资人看的场景；18:45 AI 软件的两种商业模式：高投入运营 vs 健身房模式；21:18 效率工具能否提供情绪价值，Steam 给我的启发；22:48 对我来说 ToB 不是值得创业的方向；24:44 吐槽创始人的虚荣心、装和愚昧之巅；28:36 看过美国 ToB 打法后对美国创业生态祛魅；30:21 AI Coding 越强，我越敬畏软件；35:58 消费产品把一件事做好就有价值；39:07 一个粗暴但有效的用户调研方法；44:00 AI 可能彻底颠覆'拿着锤子找钉子'；51:02 传播乐观：软件仍有巨大潜力；55:38 抵制 AI 圈的'全球首个 xxx'和番茄小说式话术；57:41 上一个产品回答的是讨好市场的证明题，现在想回答真正的开放题；1:01:37 灵魂拷问：离开字节创业后悔吗；1:05:00 创业不该过度依赖左脑。约 69 分钟。

item.title: [Lenny's Podcast] Pricing your AI product: Lessons from 400+ companies and 50 unicorns | Madhavan Ramanujam
item.description:
WHY YOU: The standard reference on how AI companies should charge, from the pricing advisor behind 400+ companies: how AI pricing differs (27:35), handling pilots that never convert (31:33), choosing the AI pricing model (38:58), and how to set up outcome-based pricing (44:48). The framework to judge every pricing story in your feed.
Madhavan Ramanujam (Simon-Kucher; Monetizing Innovation / Scaling Innovation) on pricing AI products. (04:30) Core thesis (09:20) Common traps (12:06) Beautifully simple pricing (15:00) Negotiations (27:35) How AI pricing is different (31:33) Handling POCs (38:58) Choosing the AI pricing model (43:13) Current trends (44:48) Outcome-based models (50:23) Packaging (53:40) Pricing axioms.

item.title: [Lenny's Podcast] How Intercom rose from the ashes by betting everything on AI | Eoghan McCabe (founder and CEO)
item.description:
WHY YOU: A candid founder turnaround, in the spirit of the Liblib episode you liked: Intercom's founder on going 'wartime', betting about $100M on AI, and building Fin and its per-resolution pricing. Pairs with the Intercom CFO episode already in your feed.
Eoghan McCabe, founder and CEO of Intercom, on how the company went from stagnation to one of the leading AI customer-service businesses by betting everything on AI: the wartime reset, the Fin AI agent and outcome-based pricing, culture and leadership changes.

item.title: [Pear Healthcare Playbook] Lessons from Jeffery Liu, Co-Founder and Co-CEO of Assort Health, on Fixing the Front Door of Healthcare with AI Agents
item.description:
WHY YOU: One of the fastest-growing AI front-office companies (specialty-specific voice agents for scheduling and triage), on what its first real deployments taught it and how it turns custom implementations per specialty into a platform. That's the scaling problem every 'we do the work' healthcare AI company hits.
Jeffery Liu, co-founder and co-CEO of Assort Health, on specialty-specific AI voice agents for patient access: how Assort started, why patient access is still hard to fix, lessons from early deployments, handling scheduling and triage complexity, scaling customized implementations into a platform, and AI patient navigation across voice and text.

item.title: [Understanding Healthcare with Zack Kanter] Payer enrollment with Megan Struxness at Bridge
item.description:
WHY YOU: The provider-side plumbing you run every day, from the head of payer ops and RCM at Bridge: how payer contracting and enrollment actually work, superbills and out-of-network claims, the limits of eligibility checks, how Bridge offers guaranteed payment, and how it gets providers enrolled and billing in about 45 days. Directly comparable to Klarity's own provider onboarding.
Megan Struxness is Head of Payer Operations and Revenue Cycle Management at Bridge, a healthcare platform that helps providers get credentialed, enrolled with payers and paid. Zack and Megan cover payer contracting, superbills, out-of-network claims, eligibility limits, guaranteed payment and onboarding providers in 45 days.

item.title: [Understanding Healthcare with Zack Kanter] Credentialing explained with Varun Krishnamurthy at Assured Health
item.description:
WHY YOU: An AI-native credentialing and enrollment company's CEO on how insurers verify providers, where the bottlenecks and closed panels really are, and when outsourcing credentialing makes sense: the build-vs-buy and pricing logic for a step that gates every new provider you add.
Varun Krishnamurthy is the co-founder and CEO of Assured Health, an AI-powered provider credentialing and enrollment company. He and Zack cover how insurers verify providers, credentialing bottlenecks, closed panels, and when outsourcing credentialing makes sense.

item.title: [Vital Signs with Jacob Effron and Nikhil Krishnan] Ep 67: Abridge Leaders on AI-Native Healthcare, Doctors Who Code, and the Future of Clinical AI
item.description:
WHY YOU: Pairs with the Abridge sales-engine episode already in your feed: how an AI-native health company is run internally (15:59), where admin AI vs. clinical AI will actually make money (21:08), and Abridge's move into payers and prior auth (24:47). Host Effron sits on Abridge's board, so expect a friendly interview.
Abridge's CEO and a clinical scientist on AI-native company operations, doctors who code, prototypes vs production, regulation and partnerships, admin vs clinical AI, payers and prior authorization, and pre-visit workflows and triage. Chapters: (0:00) Intro (6:30) Doctors Who Code (9:07) Prototypes vs Production (15:59) AI Native Company Ops (21:08) Admin vs Clinical AI (24:47) Payers and Prior Auth (35:19) Context, Autonomy, and Demand (40:40) Pre-visit Workflows and Triage.

item.title: [张小珺Jùn｜商业访谈录] 130. 张月光创业两年首次访谈：妙鸭不是AI Native产品、流程到上下文设计、One Way Door和乙女游戏 [中文]
item.description:
WHY YOU: Same honesty as the Liblib episode you liked: the 妙鸭 founder's first interview in two years, admitting his breakout AI product wasn't actually AI-native, what he got wrong about what lasts after a viral hit, and how he thinks about irreversible bets now. Over three hours, so it fits a long hike.
张小珺对谈张月光（妙鸭相机创始人），创业两年后首次长访谈：妙鸭为什么不是 AI Native 产品、从流程设计到上下文设计、One Way Door 式的不可逆决策，以及新方向乙女游戏。

item.title: [The GTMnow Podcast] Legora's CRO: $3.5M to $200M+ ARR, the Fastest Direct Sales Motion | Patrick Forquer
item.description:
WHY YOU: The sales-side mechanics behind the legal-AI company you track, from the CRO who took Legora from $3.5M to $200M ARR: a pilot designed so customers keep what they build (24:00), hiring 2-to-1 post-sale and the forward-deploy structure (15:30), time-to-value as the leading indicator of revenue (18:30), and the shift to consumption pricing (56:00). Chapter marks come from the feed and run slightly past the 52-minute audio, so treat them as order rather than exact. Show sponsor is Nooks, unrelated to the guest.
Legora grew from $3.5M to more than $100M in revenue in roughly a year, which the show calls the fastest a direct-sales motion has gone from zero to $100M, then doubled in under six months to $200M ARR. Patrick Forquer spent seven years at Braze, from its early days through the IPO, before joining Legora, a vertical legal-AI company backed by Benchmark and Redpoint, when it was at $3.5M in revenue. He walks through that scaling journey: his three criteria for joining a company (founder, product, investors), why time-to-value is the number-one leading indicator of revenue, the pilot design that lets customers keep what they build, forward-deployed team structure, the Jude Law and Aaron Judge brand campaigns and how brand ROI was measured, the '8 Mile' approach to competitive objections, screening sales hires for AI fluency, and the move to consumption pricing. Chapters: 0:00 Intro; 1:08 Leaving Braze for Legora at $3.5M; 1:40 The three criteria; 4:30 Assessing a founder; 6:40 Advice for operators joining AI-native companies; 9:10 Early days and first US pipeline; 12:00 From $3.5M to over $100M; 13:10 The two biggest GTM unlocks; 15:30 Hiring 2-to-1 post-sale and forward-deploy structure; 18:30 Time-to-value as the leading indicator; 21:00 Forward-deployed engineers for your own product; 24:00 Pilot design; 28:00 Shipping cadence; 30:00 A full sales tech-stack overhaul mid-scale; 32:30 The Jude Law campaign; 36:00 The Aaron Judge and Yankees partnership; 38:30 Measuring brand ROI; 47:00 What a great AE at Legora does differently; 50:00 Screening for AI fluency; 52:00 Competitive objections and the '8 Mile' framework; 56:00 The shift to consumption pricing; 58:00 Rapid fire. Hosted by Sophie Buonassisi (GTMfund). Sponsored by Nooks.

item.title: [The a16z Show] OpenAI: When AI Agents Use Computers Faster Than You [wildcard]
item.description:
WHY YOU: Every RCM and prior-auth workflow you evaluate ends up in a payer portal or EHR screen with no API. OpenAI's computer-use team on why agents that drive software through the screen are now at a scaling point, how they are being put against legacy ERP-style systems, why the harness around the model matters more than the model, and the deterministic guardrails enterprises set around them. Lab-side and a16z-hosted, so no pricing numbers; a wildcard for the mechanics behind the next generation of back-office agents.
OpenAI's Ari Weinstein and James Sun argue that computer-use agents, which operate software without APIs, are entering a scaling phase. They join a16z's Seema Amble and Fabrizio Serafini to discuss agents working with legacy ERP systems, why the harness around a model matters, and how enterprises can set deterministic guardrails. They also look ahead to agents that work in the background and adapt to users rather than requiring users to adapt to them.

item.title: [Get Paid with Manny Medina] How Intercom's CFO Bet the Business on Outcome-Based Pricing
item.description:
WHY YOU: The CFO who actually signed off on Intercom's per-resolution pricing for Fin, on the parts that matter to you: why a simple outcome price beat a cleverer one, how he trades model sophistication against unit economics, and how seller comp was rebuilt so reps would push the AI plan without eroding margin. The finance-side view of outcome-based pricing that the founder interviews skip.
Episode 50 of Get Paid. Host Manny Medina talks with Dan Griggs, Chief Financial Officer of Intercom, about how outcome-based pricing changes the economics of AI agents, why simple pricing beats complex pricing, and the strategic decisions behind SaaS companies' shift to charging for AI-powered work. Covered: moving from perpetual licenses to subscriptions while managing debt covenants; why outcome-based pricing may be the most sustainable model for AI agents; balancing AI model sophistication against unit economics; leading with principles in uncharted markets; designing seller compensation that drives transformation without destroying margins. Griggs's background includes electrical engineering, finance rotations at AT&T and Nestle, scaling Rocket Fuel from pre-IPO to over $400M in revenue, and Sitecore under private-equity ownership; at Intercom he pioneered outcome-based pricing for AI agents.

item.title: [Lifers with Christina Farr] Healthcare runs a 1980s model in 2026 | Aaron Miri, Baptist Health
item.description:
WHY YOU: The buyer's side of every pitch you make: a health system's chief digital officer on which back-office roles AI has already stopped him hiring (no help-desk hire in 18 months), what it would take to get claims paid same-day, why payer friction and liability still slow deployment, and how a system decides what it will actually pay for clinical AI. Journalist-hosted, no sponsor on this one.
Christina Farr talks with Aaron Miri, executive VP and chief digital and innovation officer at Baptist Health, about how AI is changing the way health systems operate and where liability, privacy law and payer friction still slow it down. Miri says Baptist hasn't hired a help desk agent in more than 18 months and expects AI to affect future hiring more than current roles, and argues for a universal patient identifier, the 'primary key' healthcare AI lacks. Timestamps: 00:00 Lead-in; 00:29 Intro; 01:22 ER experience breakdown; 03:39 Fixing intake friction; 06:26 Clinical AI shortcuts; 10:04 Liability and tort reform; 14:04 Universal patient ID debate; 20:54 Patients versus clinician AI; 24:50 Automation and admin jobs; 27:42 Automation shrinks the back office; 29:18 Claims and same-day payment; 33:20 Cutting costs without knee-jerk moves; 35:50 Profit pools and public programs; 39:06 Ending payer-provider resentment; 43:57 Free markets and funding innovation; 46:45 Paying for clinical AI; 48:26 Good-enough AI in practice; 50:59 AI risk versus the status quo; 53:03 Wrap.

item.title: [Lifers with Christina Farr] Healthcare AI works best on jobs no one thought to do | Hippocratic AI CEO Munjal Shah
item.description:
WHY YOU: A founder selling AI agents into health systems explains his actual price (per-minute, at 31:53), the ROI cases he closes with (three cancers found for $1,700 of AI cost in a screening-outreach run; 50,000 heat-wave calls), his traction numbers (26:41) and the copilot/autopilot/'infinite pilot' framing for which jobs AI should own outright. Pricing mechanics for selling labor-replacing AI to hospitals.
Christina Farr talks with Munjal Shah, co-founder and CEO of Hippocratic AI, about whether clinical AI will shrink healthcare's workforce and who is responsible when it errs. Shah lays out his Copilot, Autopilot and Infinite Pilot framework and argues the best results come from tasks healthcare never tried, such as calling 50,000 people during a New York heat wave; he also cites a lung cancer screening outreach that found three cancers for $1,700 in AI costs. Timestamps: 00:00 Lead-in; 00:42 Intro; 01:51 AI extinction-panic weekend; 04:47 Healthcare as an AI risk target; 06:56 Hippocratic's safety system; 09:20 Avoiding the AI-doctor trap; 12:34 Sponsor: Granola; 13:33 Liability and taking responsibility; 16:08 Redundancy and the clinical team; 18:30 Whether AI will shrink healthcare jobs; 20:38 Infinite Pilot ROI examples; 26:41 Business traction and growth metrics; 31:53 Per-minute pricing; 34:36 Fixing AI PR with specifics; 40:06 Wrap. Episode sponsor: Granola (meeting notes).

item.title: [42章经] 一个 Personal Agent 创业者的思考｜对谈 Ambi 创始人子皓 [中文] [wildcard]
item.description:
WHY YOU: An operator who ran Plaud's China business and a large-revenue company before founding a personal-agent startup, on whether agent cost is really the obstacle (10:07), how much real demand exists (11:39), why needs tied to money or status are easier to sell because the ROI is legible (14:45), why AI-coworker adoption is slower than expected (17:06), and how to make money from businesses that don't look promising (47:28). Consumer-side, hence the wildcard tag, but the demand/ROI reasoning transfers.
42章经主播曲凯对谈 Ambi 创始人莫子皓（前 Plaud 合伙人及中国区 CEO，米公益创始人（后被轻松筹收购），曾任暖哇科技、百川智能医疗业务产品与运营负责人）。上半部分聊 Personal Agent：01:49 为什么 Personal Agent 现在火了；05:58 去年'智能已经够用'的假设可能错了；10:07 成本是不是真障碍；11:39 真实需求有多少；14:45 和钱、地位绑定的需求更好做，ROI 清楚；17:06 为什么 AI 同事的落地比预期慢；18:34 转向 B 端是不是过度模仿硅谷；19:18 大厂会不会赢；21:10 Personal Agent 是否天然缺乏网络效应；24:16 快评 Town、Grok Bot、Muse、Instinct；32:31 Ambi 如何与 Muse 之类竞争；40:25 应用公司自己训模型。下半部分聊经营与心法：42:49 经营过大营收业务、模型公司和消费硬件公司的核心体会；47:28 不被看好的生意如何赚钱；50:31 生意的本质；57:01 什么人会招人；1:03:04 最大的焦虑是速度；1:04:56 硬件的优势从哪来；1:08:57 这一波最大的机会；1:11:51 '主动式'产品设计的常见错误；1:18:36 亿级用户产品的时机到了吗；1:21:08 为什么中国 AI 产品跑出来的少。

item.title: [The Heart of Healthcare] From Early Struggles to Billion+ Exit | SmarterDx Founders Michael Gao & Joshua Geleris
item.description:
WHY YOU: The founders of the largest AI-coding exit in healthcare on the part that matters to you: 18 months without a customer, the pre-bill review workflow that made contingency (share-of-recovered-revenue) pricing possible, AI translating clinical notes into billing codes now beating the average human coder, and why they'd pick a flywheel over a 'moat'. Short, but it is the economics behind every contingency-priced AI RCM pitch. Host Steve Kraus is a Bessemer partner and Bessemer backed SmarterDx; flag it if you'd rather exclude investor-host episodes.
Building a healthcare startup is harder than most people acknowledge. SmarterDx, now one of the largest health AI exits to date, went about 18 months without a customer, pursued a pivot that seemed to make little product sense, and saw its co-founders return to hospitalist shifts to cover expenses. Host Steve Kraus talks with CEO Dr. Michael Gao and Head of Product Dr. Joshua Geleris about those struggles, what finally drove growth, and the billion-plus acquisition by New Mountain Capital. Topics: why the first product idea failed and what customer objections taught them; the workflow that made contingency pricing possible; how AI translating clinical notes into billing codes now outperforms the average human, and what that means for coders and nurses; why a flywheel is a better model than a moat; and what they would change about the acquisition process. Gao was previously Medical Director for Transformation at NewYork-Presbyterian and holds faculty roles at Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai and Weill Cornell Medicine; Geleris was an Assistant Professor of Medicine at Columbia University, where NIH and DoD funded his clinical informatics work, and led Epic implementation for providers. Episode 245.

item.title: [Training Data] Box's Aaron Levie: On Reinventing Yourself in the AI Age and Enterprise Diffusion
item.description:
WHY YOU: A public-company CEO on the margin question under every AI-services business: lab token subsidies can't last, so who absorbs the cost when they end, and why he thinks a model-agnostic application layer that routes tokens keeps the customer relationship (06:56 will the labs move up the stack; 12:34 betting the company on AI; 48:00 why coding diffused fast and other knowledge work hasn't). Diffusion, not model quality, as the gating constraint on enterprise AI revenue.
Aaron Levie, cofounder and CEO of Box, describes transforming a public company around AI and building an application-layer agent harness tuned to Box's file system, permissions, and search. He argues that lab token subsidies cannot last and that enterprises benefit from a model-agnostic company routing their tokens, and explains why coding adopted AI faster than other knowledge work. Timestamps: 0:00 Introduction; 1:55 Are application companies the hottest neolabs?; 6:56 Will the labs move up the stack?; 12:34 Box and betting the company on AI; 16:50 Hero use cases; 18:42 Work slop; 24:08 Building Box's agentic harness and the evals that matter; 27:23 The state of the model race; 29:25 Open-weight model adoption in the enterprise; 32:34 Memory, continual learning, and what belongs in the weights; 37:29 Box Labs and systems of record; 44:55 Will chat be the dominant UI?; 48:00 Why coding diffused fast; 54:31 Staying wired in and making a company AI-first. Hosted by Sequoia Capital.

item.title: [The a16z Show] The Missing Infrastructure for AI Agents: Documents | Reducto's Adit Abraham [wildcard]
item.description:
WHY YOU: Every prior-auth, claims and denials agent you evaluate is downstream of this problem: messy faxes, scans and PDFs. Reducto's CEO (billions of pages a month; the seven-billionth landed the morning of recording) explains why OCR fails, why frontier models silently drop fields on long extraction jobs, and how a vision-model-plus-infrastructure layer is sold into healthcare, insurance, legal and finance. Infrastructure, not an operator story, hence the wildcard tag.
Reducto co-founder and CEO Adit Abraham joins a16z General Partner Jennifer Li to argue that document understanding is a missing layer for AI agents in healthcare, legal, finance, and insurance. They discuss why traditional OCR struggles with messy documents, how Reducto pairs vision-language models with specialized infrastructure, and why frontier models can silently drop information on long extraction tasks. Reducto processes billions of pages monthly and reached its seven billionth page the morning of the recording. a16z disclosures apply.

item.title: [Invest Like the Best] Christina Cacioppo - Building an Enduring Software Company in the Age of AI [EP.496]
item.description:
WHY YOU: A CEO with 16,000+ customers on exactly the mechanics you track: why Vanta absorbs the AI inference cost instead of passing it through (07:39), the search for an outcome-pricing unit customers will sign (10:35), and why forward-deployed engineers are a problem rather than a GTM model (27:54). Agent-first product reasoning at 05:41. Disclosure: Vanta is also an Invest Like the Best sponsor — tell me if that should disqualify sponsor-guest episodes on strong-host shows.
Patrick O'Shaughnessy talks with Christina Cacioppo, founder and CEO of Vanta, whose security and compliance platform serves more than 16,000 companies. Five years after their first conversation, they cover how Vanta won a crowded category, how a successful software business gets reinvented for AI, her bet on agents that do the work rather than assist users, the changing economics of software, the competition for top talent, AI's effect on cybersecurity, and building a lasting company in fast-moving Silicon Valley. Timestamps: 00:00:00 How Vanta Won a Crowded Category; 00:03:12 Living Through the Software Selloff; 00:05:41 Building an Agent-First Product; 00:07:39 Why Vanta Eats the Cost of AI; 00:10:35 The Search for Outcome Pricing; 00:14:31 Getting People to Actually Use AI; 00:17:46 Why Comp for Top People Is Up 10X; 00:22:13 Valuations, Tenders, and the Endgame; 00:24:20 What's Overhyped and Underhyped; 00:27:54 The Problem With FDEs; 00:29:34 Why French Startups Use Chinese Models; 00:30:22 Vanta as a Security Company; 00:36:57 What Makes a Great Talk; 00:40:14 Where She Would Invest Today; 00:45:19 The Billboard War; 00:49:35 The AI Trust Crisis; 00:51:39 Security Five Years From Now.

item.title: [The a16z Show] What Happens When Al Agents Can Spend Your Money?
item.description:
WHY YOU: Town started as an AI-powered tax service for small businesses — a services-as-software bet — and Jean-Denis Grèze explains why he walked away from it for a personal assistant that does the work across email, calendar and business workflows, and why model neutrality and owning the data matter once the labs compete with application companies. A pivot story from inside the services-as-software camp; the notes promise no pricing numbers, so take it for the strategy, with Rampell asking the business-model questions.
Town CEO Jean-Denis Grèze argues that AI transformed coding faster than everyday work because the bottleneck is making AI usable for people who lack the time or technical skill to build their own automations, not raw intelligence. He and a16z General Partner Alex Rampell discuss Town's move from tax software to a personal AI assistant built around email, calendars and business workflows; why consumer-grade experiences may win in enterprise AI; how Town finds and automates tasks users would not think to delegate; why model neutrality and data ownership matter as AI labs increasingly compete with application companies; what happens when agents act on people's behalf in everyday work, shopping and commerce; and why software may need to adapt to each user rather than the reverse. Resources: Alex Rampell on X (x.com/arampell); Jean-Denis Grèze on X (x.com/jgreze); Town (town.com). a16z disclosures apply.

item.title: [十字路口Crossing] 新的创业机会，正在 Claude Code 和 Codex 周围长出来｜对谈 Treg [中文] [wildcard]
item.description:
WHY YOU: Three pivots in nine months, told with what killed each one: a design agent dropped because the models ate it (04:59), a fully automated growth agent that did lots of work but produced no growth (17:36), and the 'zero-person company' assumption that didn't hold (06:59, 35:01). Ends on what agents actually pay for (18:04) and a Costco-style model for selling to agents (21:57). Adjacent to your core, but the most candid failure-and-pivot talk this week.
本期嘉宾是 Treg 创始人 Jason Zhou 和创始工程师石天鑫。九个多月里他们经历了三次转向：从设计 Agent SuperDesign，到全自动增长 Agent，再到为 Agent 提供数据与工具的 Treg。聊到垂直 Agent 为什么处境艰难、「零人公司」为什么比看起来更难、AI 干了很多活为什么不等于增长、围绕 Coding Agent 长出来的产品（Ego、ChatCut），以及同时跑多个 Agent 时人反而成为瓶颈。章节：02:18 九个月三次转向：SuperDesign、增长 Agent、Treg；03:10 从周末项目到 6000+ GitHub stars；04:59 模型吃掉应用：为什么放弃 SuperDesign；06:59 「零人公司」浪潮是个错误假设；14:42 一个 Codex 插件意外改变了增长曲线；17:36 从增长 Agent 里抽出最有价值的一层；18:04 Agent 最常买什么工具；20:13 浏览器抓不到的数据是工具市场的价值；21:57 为什么 Treg 更像 Costco；23:39 应用公司的数据飞轮；25:38 三次转向的教训：建在 Claude Code 和 Codex 之上；26:43 Ego (lite) 与 ChatCut；31:56 从 Vibe Island 到 Orca：多 Agent 时代的机会；34:25 转向期两个月不做产品；35:01 「零人公司」为什么不成立；36:18 怎么做 Loop Engineering；38:50 同时跑 5–10 个 session，人成了瓶颈；40:13 Claude Code 还是 Codex；41:41 Grok Bot 与云端沙盒；43:22 国产模型、视频模型、快模型各自适合的场景；45:08 当程序员写不过 AI；47:15 三次转向中最想放弃的时刻；49:05 Fail fast；49:22 相信 AGI 会来为什么还要创业；50:28 即使有通用模型，仍然需要更好的工具。

item.title: [GTM Science] How Abridge Built an AI-Powered Enterprise Sales Engine with Jeremy Von Halle
item.description:
WHY YOU: How a $200M+ AI-healthcare company actually runs enterprise sales into ~300 health systems: a 200-person commercial org for 300 accounts (06:36), the save-time → save-money → make-money ROI arc on an 18-month cycle (09:33, 11:26), and centralized AI builds vs. rep-built tools (16:33). The GTM mechanics the Abridge CEO interviews skip.
Host Eddie Reynolds talks with Jeremy Von Halle, VP of Revenue Operations and Chief of Staff to the Chief Commercial Officer at Abridge. Abridge grew from two sellers and under $5M ARR to over $200M in revenue selling into a market of about 300 large health systems. Jeremy walks through the AI-driven rev-ops engine behind that growth: prepping sellers before calls, routing insights from conversations, completing RFPs in under an hour, monitoring all 300 accounts for news, and scoring deal risk — plus Archie, Abridge's internal AI agent in Salesforce and Slack, an ROI framework for long sales cycles, and the case for centralized AI builds over rep-built tools. Timestamps: 00:23 Intro to Jeremy Von Halle and Abridge; 02:48 Why AI in enterprise sales is about depth, not breadth; 06:36 A 200-person commercial org selling into only 300 accounts; 09:33 Save time, save money, make money: the ROI arc; 11:26 When and how to prove ROI with an 18-month sales cycle; 15:39 The QA layer: flagging calls that don't meet the rubric; 16:33 Centralized AI build vs. reps vibe-coding their own solutions; 25:08 How many iterations before you get it right?; 28:19 The foundational data layer; 30:59 Capturing call transcripts and updating Salesforce; 32:10 Golden and rotten events: sentiment signals from interactions; 36:55 Archie: the AI agent embedded in Salesforce and Slack; 40:28 Daily news monitoring across all 300 accounts; 40:58 RFP completion from days to under an hour; 43:23 AI-powered forecast prep for frontline managers; 44:48 Deal risk scoring from conversational and stage-progression data.

item.title: [Understanding Healthcare with Zack Kanter] Medicaid and Medicare with Neil Batlivala at Pair Team
item.description:
WHY YOU: How money actually flows through Medicaid and Medicare (08:05), why state-by-state programs make it hard to build one product (10:22), and how a provider org uses AI care managers plus agentic verification (22:31) to make whole-person Medicaid care pencil out. The payment-flow mechanics under any AI product sold into Medicaid-heavy practices; CMS's ACCESS model at 40:22.
Neil Batlivala is co-founder and CEO of Pair Team, a provider organization offering team-guided, AI-enabled care navigation for Medicaid patients. Neil and Zack cover how Medicaid programs pay providers, why medical care and social services remain fragmented for patients who need both, why Pair Team chose Medicaid over commercial insurance as its first lane, how it finds patients, how it uses AI care managers and agentic verification to lower the cost of whole-person care, and how Medicare's ACCESS model fits in. Chapters: 00:00 Introduction; 00:20 What does Pair Team do?; 01:37 What did Medicaid patients do before Pair Team?; 06:54 Why did Pair Team choose Medicaid over commercial insurance?; 08:05 How does money flow through Medicare and Medicaid?; 10:22 Why is it hard to innovate across state Medicaid programs?; 12:48 How did Pair Team pick Medicaid as its first lane?; 19:31 How does Pair Team find its patients?; 22:31 How does Pair Team use AI agents?; 27:49 Having AI agents prompt the person; 31:35 Where does Medicaid coverage miss what patients need?; 36:26 Who can Pair Team serve, and who can't?; 40:22 What is CMS's ACCESS model for Medicare?; 46:56 What's one thing Neil would change about U.S. healthcare?

item.title: [晚点聊 LateTalk] 175: 对话Liblib陈冕：关于活下来，以及所有接近死亡的时刻 [中文]
item.description:
WHY YOU: A founder running >$300M ARR across Liblib/Lovart/LibTV defends being accused of buying growth with aggressive pricing: the subsidy/blow-up rumours (4:10), how LibTV membership pricing was set (11:01), the near-collapse (1:08:36) and how an AI app survives as models absorb its value (1:28:10). Rare candid failure-and-unit-economics talk from a Chinese AI-app operator.
晚点聊对话演语科技 Evoken 创始人陈冕。演语科技旗下有 Liblib、Lovart、LibTV 三个产品，ARR 超过 3 亿美元，在 AI 应用融资最艰难的时候以 20 亿美元估值一笔融了 3 亿美元；围绕它的争议也同时达到顶峰：缺少原创、靠激进定价换增长、不够技术、迟早会爆雷。这场对话追问的是：在一个模型不断吞噬应用价值的时代，一家 AI 应用公司如何活下来。章节：4:10 爆雷与补贴传闻；11:01 LibTV 会员定价；21:42 早期融资压力；34:51 原创性争议；49:20 管理与核心团队离开；1:08:36 最接近死亡的时刻；1:28:10 在模型厂商之间活下来；2:05:55 三年复盘。

item.title: [The a16z Show] Why Real-World AI Is Harder Than the Benchmark | EliseAI's Mario Martone [wildcard]
item.description:
WHY YOU: Short one: an operator running AI front-office agents for housing and healthcare on why production reliability (and the cost of a wrong answer on a patient or tenant call) is a different problem from benchmark scores. The operating reality behind every 'we do the work' front-office pitch you'll evaluate.
Mario Martone of EliseAI explains why AI errors in housing and healthcare demand more reliability than benchmark scores suggest. He covers EliseAI's call volume, what breaks when agents meet real tenants and patients, and how the company combines different AI methods to get reliability in production.

item.title: [Understanding Healthcare with Zack Kanter] Dental billing with Mike Huffaker at Planet DDS
item.description:
WHY YOU: Dental is a preview of where practice-side RCM is heading: groups consolidating onto one stack, dental providers submitting medical claims, eligibility data so thin that practices still phone payers for estimates — and a CRO explaining why every health-tech company ends up in RCM (33:54). Kanter pushes on mechanics.
Mike Huffaker is Chief Revenue Officer at Planet DDS, a cloud-based, AI-enabled practice management and imaging platform built for large dental groups, and host of The Dental Economist Show. He and Zack cover why dental groups are moving to a single tech stack, why more dental providers are submitting medical claims, why incomplete payer eligibility data still leaves practices calling insurers for cost estimates, and why dental claims still go out in end-of-day batches. Chapters: 00:00 Introduction; 00:24 What Planet DDS does; 01:37 What dental groups are switching away from; 04:32 What distinguishes software built for multi-location groups; 06:40 What happens when a DSO acquires a practice; 11:44 How DSO consolidation changed dental software; 18:58 What dental groups integrate with; 22:39 Why dental providers need to submit medical claims; 26:50 How medical claims differ from dental claims; 33:54 Why nearly every health tech company ends up in RCM; 39:01 Why estimating dental costs across payers is so hard; 45:00 Whether payers benefit from billing friction; 50:21 What Mike would change about dental RCM.

item.title: [Invest Like the Best] Gabe Stengel - Building Investing Superintelligence - [Invest Like the Best, EP.492]
item.description:
WHY YOU: A vertical-AI CEO on moving from seat to outcome pricing (23:43) and how firms actually buy AI (22:00), with the enterprise-sales motion spelled out (32:55) — the finance analogue of Harvey/Legora, from the operator rather than an investor.
Gabe Stengel is co-founder and CEO of Rogo, an AI platform for finance. He argues the best investors will spend the next several years reorganizing their firms around AI. The conversation covers how Rogo evolved alongside frontier models, why the last mile and the software harness around the models matter, what happens when every portfolio manager can run thousands of agents on a problem, how AI could change how capital is raised, how assets are priced and how deals get done, the move from seat-based to outcome-based pricing, which investing skills gain value as AI improves, Rogo's internal company brain (Shrek), the 40 investor rejections before the Series A, the aggressiveness applied AI requires, and how to become a magnet for talent and capital. Timestamps: 00:00:00 Welcome; 00:01:24 The model eras of Rogo; 00:04:15 The last mile; 00:06:14 Who uses Rogo today; 00:10:55 Which investor skills matter; 00:12:23 The data stack; 00:14:33 Competing with frontier labs; 00:16:57 The harness; 00:18:05 Who wins in vertical AI; 00:22:00 How firms buy AI; 00:23:43 From seats to outcome pricing; 00:31:19 Auditability vs. accuracy; 00:32:55 Enterprise sales; 00:34:48 Shrek; 00:35:49 The pitch to talent; 00:42:18 The Series A rejections; 00:47:41 Finance's innovator's dilemma; 00:50:22 Questions firms should ask; 00:53:09 What remains uncertain; 00:56:46 Becoming a talent black hole; 00:57:56 The kindest thing.

item.title: [The a16z Show] Why AI Could Finally Fix Healthcare Access | Zocdoc CEO Oliver Kharraz
item.description:
WHY YOU: An incumbent front door turning its scheduling layer into infrastructure for AI agents, insurers and other platforms (the Gemini deal). If agents become the patient's entry point, the front-office stack you sell to practices changes shape — worth hearing how Zocdoc plans to be paid for that.
Why is booking a doctor's appointment still so hard, and can AI finally fix it? Zocdoc CEO Oliver Kharraz argues the problem isn't finding doctors; it's connecting patients to accurate availability and making appointments bookable from wherever a patient starts. a16z General Partner Julie Yoo and Oliver discuss how Zocdoc spent nearly two decades building the infrastructure for online scheduling and is now opening that technology to AI agents, insurers and other platforms. They cover Zocdoc's partnership with Gemini, why patients shouldn't be locked into a single healthcare platform, how surfacing last-minute openings can cut waits from weeks to days, what changes when AI becomes a new front door to healthcare, and why Zocdoc's future extends well beyond its own app. Resources: Oliver Kharraz on LinkedIn; Julie Yoo on X. a16z disclosures apply.

item.title: [20VC] $1BN ARR in 18 Months; The Untold Story of Higgsfield | Spending $4M Per Month on Models | Why Moats in AI are BS | Scaling a Content Team to 150 People with Alex Mashrabov [wildcard]
item.description:
WHY YOU: The most concrete AI-app unit-economics numbers this month: a $1B run-rate in 18 months set against ~$4M a month in model spend (28:00), and a founder arguing moats and 'wrapper' worries are beside the point (36:00). Consumer video, not services — but the margin math transfers.
Alex Mashrabov is the founder and CEO of Higgsfield, described as the third-fastest company to reach $1BN in ARR behind OpenAI and Anthropic, with reports of a new round at roughly $8BN. He previously sold his company to Snap for $166M and was a top-three competitive programmer as a child. Topics: 00:00 From programming prodigy to the $166M sale to Snap; 09:00 Burning through $10M and the pivot that saved Higgsfield; 12:00 Is the $1BN run-rate in 18 months real?; 16:00 Will OpenAI and Google wipe out $20 consumer AI subscriptions?; 21:00 Are AI labs gaming benchmarks?; 28:00 Spending roughly $4M a month on models — smart or reckless?; 36:00 Are AI moats overstated, and the 'wrapper' debate; 43:00 Time with his son and what ambition costs; 54:00 Quickfire: is Snap in trouble, can HubSpot survive AI; 01:02:00 The plan to reach $10BN in revenue within 12 months.

item.title: [Understanding Healthcare with Zack Kanter] Agentic AI for the revenue cycle with Ayo Omojola at Substrate
item.description:
WHY YOU: The clearest walk-through I found of how an AI-native RCM company actually operates: why Substrate dropped browser automation for agents, why payers still mail critical info, and big payers vs. the long tail. Host built Stedi, so he pushes on mechanics.
Ayo Omojola is the co-founder and CEO of Substrate, an AI agent platform for revenue cycle automation. Before starting Substrate, Ayo saw the friction firsthand working in primary and urgent care. In this episode, Ayo explains why Substrate moved from browser automation to agentic AI, why there's so much friction in the revenue cycle, and how healthcare billing could be 5x faster and cheaper with current tools.

item.title: [Understanding Healthcare with Zack Kanter] Revenue recovery with Eliana Berger at Joyful Health
item.description:
WHY YOU: AI recovery of denied/unpaid claims without changing the practice's systems — recovery rates and cost-to-collect are the unit economics behind the contingency-fee AI RCM model.
Eliana Berger is co-founder and CEO of Joyful Health. Eliana and Zack discuss revenue recovery – how healthcare practices lose revenue through unpaid insurance claims. Eliana explains denials management, why fixing denials requires more than just filing appeals, and how Joyful Health's AI platform recovers that revenue without requiring practices to change their existing systems.

item.title: [Vital Signs with Jacob Effron and Nikhil Krishnan] Ep 66: Pete Shalek On The Future of Front Office Automation
item.description:
WHY YOU: AI front office for independent practices sold as 'we do the work' rather than software — pricing, 3–4 week implementations, 5–7% conversion lift. Directly relevant to how you sell to and onboard providers.
Pete Shalek, founder of Valerie Health, is a multi-time healthcare entrepreneur who previously founded Joyable and served as Chief Product Officer at AbleTo and Stellar Health. Pete discusses why AI in healthcare needs to move beyond selling software tools to actually doing the work for providers.

item.title: [Get Paid with Manny Medina] Same AI, Wildly Different Price: What Separates $50 From $5M with Jaya Gupta [wildcard]
item.description:
WHY YOU: Post-mortem of the outcome-based pricing thesis: what held up, where token costs and trust decide price. Medina builds billing for agents, so it stays concrete.
Episode 57: host Manny Medina sits down with Jaya Gupta from Foundation Capital to discuss AI startups, context graphs, token maxing, and outcome-based pricing, exploring what's really working six months after her viral paper.

item.title: [Cheeky Pint] Bret Taylor of Sierra on AI agents, outcome-based pricing, and the OpenAI board
item.description:
WHY YOU: Directly answers how Sierra charges: outcome vs seat pricing, from the founder, with a numbers-minded host.
Bret Taylor, co-founder of Sierra and Chair of the OpenAI board, joins John for a pint to discuss the rapid shift toward an agentic future. In this episode, Bret explains why outcome-based pricing is the future of software business models, and why he believes the atomic unit of AI productivity is a process, not a person. They cover why big companies struggle to adopt AI because they are “shipping their org charts.” Bret also discusses a new type of hyper-generalist, reflects on his experience with the OpenAI and Twitter boards, and explains why he believes we might see the end of the smartphone era. Jacob and Logan sit down with Max Junestrand, founder and CEO of Legora - a rapidly growing legal AI platform (and Redpoint portfolio company). item.title: [The a16z Show] Healthcare 2026: AI Doctors, GLP-1s, and Insurance Defection
item.description:
WHY YOU: Broadest of the batch: a16z's read on where healthcare money moves in 2026. No RCM/EHR episode cleared the bar yet, so this holds the healthcare slot.
Out-of-Pocket is a healthcare education company founded by Nikhil Krishnan that helps people understand how healthcare works and how to navigate it in practice. In this episode, a16z investing partner Jay Rughani and Nikhil discuss why health insurance is losing its role as the default way people access care. They explain how rising costs are pushing more consumers to pay out of pocket for diagnostics, preventive care, and navigation. The conversation also looks at what this shift means for startups, AI-powered tools, regulation, and access as healthcare continues to move beyond insurance. item.title: [十字路口Crossing] “我们首先要贵！” ——定价200美金/月才能验证AI市场刚需｜对谈郭振宇：Sandwich Lab创始人/CEO [中文] [wildcard]
